Thank you. Thank you so much to the European Commission. And I'm turning to Canada next. Ms. Andrea Sherston, Director for Environment and Climate Change, can I ask you for your intervention, please?

Thank you. Thank you so much, Canada. And also, as a co-chair of the Global Methane Pledge, thank you for your leadership. I turn to Kazakhstan next. Mr. Dida Temenov, Director General of the Department of Multilateral Cooperation, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Sir, you have the floor.

Mr. Elchin Alaverdiyev, head of the Climate Diplomacy Department in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The floor is yours, sir.

Thank you, Martin, and good afternoon, dear colleagues. As both an energy-producing country and also holding once a COP presidency, We believe that methane action should deliver several objectives at the same time, such as reducing emissions, improving efficiency, strengthening energy security, and supporting economic development. For Azerbaijan, the oil and gas sector offers some of the most immediate opportunities for methane reductions. This is also where Azerbaijan is already taking concrete actions. We have submitted our NDC 3.0 last year and advanced our 2050 targets by 15 years where the methane sector holds very significant share of the reductions. In 2022, the oil and gas sector accounted for around 29% of Azerbaijan's total greenhouse gas emissions, with methane from venting and fugitive emissions among the main sources. Azerbaijan joined the Global Methane Pledge in 2024, and the SOCAR, the national energy company, has established medium and long-term objectives for its directly operated assets, including eliminating routine flaring by 2030, reducing upstream emissions intensity by 30% by 2030, and achieving near zero upstream methane intensity below 0.2% by 2035. Furthermore, SOKA joined OGMP 2.0 in 2024 and submitted its first report in 2025. It has also developed an advanced MRV system and the Methane AI platform, bringing together data from satellites, drones, and other sources to strengthen methane measurement and mitigation. It's also worthwhile to underline the strong regional cooperation to accelerate methane abatement. In 2025, SOCAR, together with KazMunGas from Kazakhstan and Uzbekneftegaz from Uzbekistan, launched the Caspian Methane Emission Accelerator, moving regional cooperation towards a practical action at operational sites. SOCAR and BP are also working to strengthen methane measurement, reporting, and mitigation capabilities among operators in Azerbaijan. Ladies and gentlemen, we recognize that methane performance is increasingly becoming a market issue. Higher standards can support stronger investment and innovation, but higher standards must be accompanied by partnership. The global low-methane energy market cannot be built only through new obligations for producers. Consumer countries, international financial institutions, and technology providers all have a role in enabling producers, particularly in developing countries, to meet higher standards. Our message is, therefore, simple. Raising ambition should be complemented and supported by creating enabling conditions for implementation. We need finance, technology, capacity building, and international cooperation to turn methane commitments into measurable reduction. This is a way making energy sector more efficient, strengthening energy security, and supporting a credible pathway to our broader climate objectives. Thank you.
I thank Azerbaijan, and I turn to Australia next, Ms. Amanda Wormald. branch head from the Department of Climate, Energy, Environment and Water. The floor is yours, please.

As other speakers have said, 1.5 degrees, despite the overshoot report that UNEP has published now, remains the ultimate aspiration of our global targets, and methane undoubtedly has a role to play in helping us achieve and minimise the overshoot to the extent possible. Within Australia, our approach has always been to take methane seriously, and as a result, it has always been covered in our all-economy, all-of-greenhouse-gases approach. It is our belief that you cannot reduce what you cannot measure, and you cannot track that which you do not report. And so, over two decades of continuous improvement and innovation, we have developed and refined world-first independent monitoring systems. We go beyond the international reporting requirements, publishing national inventory updates by gas, including methane, and by sector every quarter. We follow the new research, data, technologies, and practices at home and abroad to further enhance the quality of our inventory. Our National Greenhouse and Energy Report scheme is one of the most technically sophisticated of its type in the world, including direct measurement methods for venting from oil and gas operations. And open-cut coal mines in Australia are increasingly applying the highest IPCC method tier. We pair this measurement, reporting, and verification with investment in actual reductions. Our safeguard mechanism is a regulatory tool that requires our biggest emitters to ratchet down their emissions, including methane, year on year. We've invested over $42 million to develop and demonstrate technologies to cut methane emissions from our coal industry. Most recently, our National Science Agency reported successful large-scale field trials at a coal mine, which achieved a 98% methane destruction efficiency using novel technology. It's this kind of investment in the pillars that will get us to the point of being able to deliver on a zero emissions or near to zero emissions methane marketplace. And I'm delighted that Australia is able to contribute in the work that it is doing on that front.

Thank you so much. Thank you so much, Australia. My next speaker is from Bloomberg Philanthropies. We have Ms. Anta Williams, who is the environment program lead. and Bloomberg Philanthropies is one of the co-conveners, actually, of the Solution Dialogue and a firm and steady supporter of methane action. Thank you.

Thank you so much, Martin.

We're really pleased to support UNEP's efforts to reduce methane emissions through MAO. So thank you for the partnership, and thanks to all the leaders around this table.

The Secretary General's call to action set.

The right target with near zero methane emissions from oil and gas, and it's the largest, as we know, cost effective reduction available to us.

And the technologies and operating practices already exist.

The challenge, as we know, is not only to improve.

Methane measurement, but to ensure that better information leads to faster mitigation. Better data can identify major emission sources more quickly and precisely, but that only matters when governments have the policies and institutions to respond and when companies act on what's been found. That's why we've expanded our methane work to strengthen the full chain from monitoring to rapid response to practical action by governments and industry. What we've learned from that work is simple. When a company's leadership is shown a map of its own leakage, it usually wants to fix it. Visibility changes behavior, but only when someone is positioned to act on what it reveals.

Looking ahead, three priorities matter most.

First is stronger policy frameworks so that methane transparency is built into regulation, public accountability, and clear expectations for action. Second, stronger implementation capacity so data reaches the institutions and decision makers who can act on it quickly and at scale.

And third, stronger industry response because companies able to address these emissions should do so with urgency. This is also the foundation for the near-zero marketplace this dialogue is working toward.

Buyers cannot reward low methane production without measurement that they can trust and compare.

Philanthropy can support all three, investing in data and the experts who translate data into actionable insights, supporting the implementation of policy and programs which identify and repair methane emissions, and convening governments, experts, industry, and civil society to drive the collaboration and progress that we need. We're entering a new era of methane visibility.

The task is now to make that transparency not only impressive, but useful, embedded in policy, translated into implementation, and matched by concrete industry action.

Thank you.

I thank Bloomberg Philanthropies, and I turn to the International Energy Agency, Ms. Sophie Westlake, who is the Senior Advisor on Multilateral Engagement and Strategy. Ms. Westlake, you have the floor, please.

Thank you so much. And, yeah, good to see everyone today and really interesting discussion. So thanks for the contributions so far. I'll try and be quite brief. A lot of what I think I would cover has already been said. As noted, the IAEA has always put out this figure that we could reduce methane emissions by some, well we now have 77 percent, so even more than three quarters, by adopting, using known technologies, existing technologies and measures on a wide scale. But the truth is that emissions in the fossil fuel sector are not decreasing despite that technology being available and despite many really good examples of how it can be deployed. So, I think the project as we see it is how do you create a framework that enables buyers to select those fuels with near zero intensity so that we can really accelerate and push that abatement process. And from our modelling that we see, If you did successfully create that signal, you created that demand for low emission gas and oil, then you could have quite an immediate effect. So we've modeled this at 20%. that if those major countries of major demand sent that signal effectively, you would see that drop of 20%. But then if you also applied that domestically, you would see that go up more significantly. So we've been working closely with the group of countries that led by the UK statement at COP30 that signaled this intent to create that near-zero methane intensity marketplace to build a voluntary framework that enables buyers to select those fuels with a near-zero intensity. And this also importantly responds to action item three of the UN Secretary General's call to action to adopt a science-based global methane standard. So we've been conducting consultations all this year with industry, governments, fossil fuel buyers, and other stakeholders. And we are developing this framework along the basis of four foundational building blocks for how you would go about building that near-zero methane intensity marketplace. And this includes what we really need is access to transparent emission performance information. We need a consistent framework for buyers to compare emission performance. And there are lots of available certificates out there or different schemes, but the point is to work together to work on a system that allows you to compare, that allows also producers to understand what they're being asked from those different importer markets. We're also, the third element of this, the building blocks is a buyer's trust in emission reporting. And then the fourth is clear incentives for buyers to select low intensity fuels. So you need to have faith as the producer that the buyer is actually wanting to buy the lower emission fuel. So to address these requirements, the IEA has developed a framework. This is based on reporting upstream methane performance at an assets level, which is an important, I think, distinction from some of the certification schemes that are available. We think that's the way to eventually go. And it also uses a dual grade system that reflects methane intensity and data quality. So you're looking at both the intensity of the methane, but you're also looking at the reliability of the data that you're getting. So, I think all of this comes together with this idea that, you know, if this group of countries is willing to move forward, we will get there by working together. And the work that we want to do over the next couple of years is very much aimed at facilitating that. Different countries can have different approaches. And I think, you know, we've talked a lot about the EU regulation, super important signal, but other countries are also doing other things, and there is a way that we can bring those all together so that we send a strong signal to the overall marketplace, but it doesn't require a unified approach. I'll leave it there. Thank you very much.

I thank the IEA for the very practical suggestion and also for your partnership along this way. I turn now to the Oil and Gas Climate Initiative, Mr. Bjorn Otto Swedrup, who is the chair of the executive committee. So the floor is yours.
